title: Positioning: why the smaller market is the bigger lever
hook: A product for everyone is noticed by no one. What positioning really is, why narrow wins first, and the research that speaks against it.

lines.text: Ask a founder who the product is for, and you often hear: basically, anyone who needs it.
It feels safe. A bigger market means more possible customers, and so more chances.
In practice, it is one of the most common reasons why a good product is not noticed at all.
Today: what positioning really is, why the smaller market is usually the bigger lever, and what research says against that.

lines.text: Positioning is often confused with a slogan or a logo. It is neither.
It is the frame you set around your product: who it is for, what it replaces, and why it is the better choice for exactly these people.
A famous case: the British drink Lucozade was sold for decades as a drink for sick people. The slogan was: Lucozade aids recovery.
In 1983, the company changed nothing important about the liquid. It changed the frame: a drink that replaces lost energy, shown with a top athlete.
Sales roughly tripled within five years. Same product, different frame, different business.

lines.text: Why does the frame matter so much? Because nobody judges a product on its own.
Within seconds, people put a new thing into a box they already know. Ah, this is something like that.
Take a chocolate muffin and a slice of chocolate cake. Almost the same recipe.
The muffin is compared to breakfast and sold in a coffee shop, for three euros. The cake is compared to dessert and sold in a restaurant, for eight.
If you do not choose the box, your customers choose it for you. And they usually pick one in which you look weak.

scenes.title: Five questions that build a position
scenes.svg:
<text x="200" y="34" class="mid ts fm" data-l="0" data-fx="up">five questions, in this order</text>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up"><rect x="24" y="52" width="352" height="44" rx="12" class="fp"/><circle cx="52" cy="74" r="13" class="fk sa"/><text x="52" y="79" class="mid ts fa tb">1</text><text x="78" y="79" class="ts">What would they use if you did not exist?</text></g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up"><rect x="24" y="106" width="352" height="44" rx="12" class="fp"/><circle cx="52" cy="128" r="13" class="fk sa"/><text x="52" y="133" class="mid ts fa tb">2</text><text x="78" y="133" class="ts">What do you have that it lacks?</text></g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up" data-d="3.5"><rect x="24" y="160" width="352" height="44" rx="12" class="fp"/><circle cx="52" cy="182" r="13" class="fk sa"/><text x="52" y="187" class="mid ts fa tb">3</text><text x="78" y="187" class="ts">What does that do for the customer?</text></g>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up"><rect x="24" y="214" width="352" height="44" rx="12" class="fp"/><circle cx="52" cy="236" r="13" class="fk sb"/><text x="52" y="241" class="mid ts fb tb">4</text><text x="78" y="241" class="ts">Who cares about that most?</text></g>
<g data-l="4" data-fx="up"><rect x="24" y="268" width="352" height="44" rx="12" class="fp"/><circle cx="52" cy="290" r="13" class="fk sa"/><text x="52" y="295" class="mid ts fa tb">5</text><text x="78" y="295" class="ts">Which category makes it obvious?</text></g>
<text x="200" y="346" class="mid ts fb tb" data-l="4" data-fx="up" data-d="3.5">the target group comes fourth, not first</text>

lines.text: The consultant April Dunford breaks positioning into five questions. The order matters.
One: what would your customers use if you did not exist? Often the honest answer is not a competitor. It is Excel, an intern, or doing nothing.
Two: what do you have that these alternatives lack? Three: what does that do for the customer, in the customer’s own words?
Four: who cares about that benefit much more than everyone else? That group is your target.
Five: which category makes all of this obvious at first glance? Notice that the target group comes fourth, not first.

quiz.q: A maker of project software keeps losing deals. The customers do not choose a rival product. They stay with Excel. What follows for its positioning?

options.text: The real alternative is Excel, so the offer must be framed against Excel
options.why: Positioning starts with what customers would otherwise use. If that is Excel, every argument has to answer one question: why is this better than my spreadsheet?

options.text: It needs more features, to clearly beat the other software makers
options.why: More features help against rival products. But the deals are not lost to rivals. Against a familiar spreadsheet, extra features can even look like extra effort.

options.text: These customers are too small, so it should aim at larger firms
options.why: Possible, but the lost deals alone do not show that. First find out why Excel wins. The cause may be the message, not the size of the customer.

options.text: It should cut its price, because Excel is already paid for
options.why: Price matters, but it comes after the frame. As long as customers see no clear advantage over Excel, even a low price is money for nothing.

quiz.explain: Imagine you sell umbrellas, and people keep walking past your stand. You look at the other umbrella stands and decide that yours need a better handle. But the people walking past are not buying umbrellas elsewhere. They pull up their hoods. Your real competitor is the hood. As long as you argue against other umbrellas, you answer a question nobody asked. The first step in positioning is to find the hood: the thing customers actually use today. Only then can you say why your offer is worth the change. Features, price and target group all come after that.

scenes.svg:
<text x="200" y="38" class="mid tm" data-l="1" data-fx="up">2,000 real contacts per year</text>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="70" width="166" height="170" rx="12" class="fp sm s1"/>
<rect x="24" y="238" width="166" height="2" class="fc"/>
<text x="107" y="150" class="mid tl tb">400,000</text><text x="107" y="174" class="mid ts fm">small firms</text>
<text x="107" y="268" class="mid tm fc tb">0.5%</text>
<text x="107" y="288" class="mid ts fm">heard once, forgotten</text>
</g>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up">
<rect x="210" y="70" width="166" height="170" rx="12" class="fp sm s1"/>
<path d="M210 155 H376 V228 Q376 240 364 240 H222 Q210 240 210 228 Z" class="fa" style="opacity:.35"/>
<text x="293" y="118" class="mid tl tb">4,000</text><text x="293" y="142" class="mid ts fm">architecture offices</text>
<text x="293" y="268" class="mid tm fa tb">50%</text>
<text x="293" y="288" class="mid ts fm">heard three or four times</text>
</g>
<g data-l="4" data-fx="up">
<text x="107" y="330" class="mid tm fc tb">invisible</text>
<text x="293" y="330" class="mid tm fa tb">well known</text>
<text x="200" y="366" class="mid ts fm">same effort, different market</text>
</g>

lines.text: Now to the size of the market. Here is a calculation that most founders never do.
Suppose your time and your budget allow two thousand real customer contacts per year.
In a market of four hundred thousand small firms, that is half a percent. Each firm hears from you once at best, and forgets it.
In a market of four thousand architecture offices, it is every second office. Many of them hear from you three or four times.
The same effort makes you invisible in one market, and well known in the other.

quiz.q: Look only at the numbers: 2,000 contacts a year, and either 4,000 architecture offices or 400,000 small firms. What speaks for the architects?

options.text: Architects will pay higher prices than the average small firm
options.why: Focus often does allow higher prices later. But that is a result of being the known specialist. The numbers themselves do not show it.

options.text: Each office can be reached several times, so the firm becomes a known name
options.why: Half the market, three or four times each: that is the difference between being a name people recognize and being one message among thousands.

options.text: Two thousand contacts are enough to sell to half of all offices
options.why: Reaching an office is not the same as selling to it. Contact creates awareness. A sale also needs a problem, a budget and trust.

options.text: A small market has fewer competitors, so it is the safer choice
options.why: Sometimes true, sometimes not. Niches can be crowded as well. And the contact numbers say nothing about competitors.

quiz.explain: Think of handing out flyers. With two thousand flyers in a big city, you could give one to every two-hundredth person. Each of them sees you once and forgets you. In a village of four thousand people, the same pile reaches every second household, and many people see your flyer at the baker, at the bus stop and in the mailbox. Nobody has bought anything yet. But in the village, people start to say: I have heard of them. That recognition is what the numbers buy you. Prices, competitors and actual sales are separate questions that the contact numbers cannot answer.

<circle cx="226" cy="118" r="19" class="fn sm s1 dash"/><circle cx="226" cy="118" r="7" class="fb"/><circle cx="270" cy="118" r="19" class="fn sm s1 dash"/><circle cx="270" cy="118" r="7" class="fb"/><circle cx="314" cy="118" r="19" class="fn sm s1 dash"/><circle cx="314" cy="118" r="7" class="fb"/><circle cx="358" cy="118" r="19" class="fn sm s1 dash"/><circle cx="358" cy="118" r="7" class="fb"/><circle cx="226" cy="170" r="19" class="fn sm s1 dash"/><circle cx="226" cy="170" r="7" class="fb"/><circle cx="270" cy="170" r="19" class="fn sm s1 dash"/><circle cx="270" cy="170" r="7" class="fb"/><circle cx="314" cy="170" r="19" class="fn sm s1 dash"/><circle cx="314" cy="170" r="7" class="fb"/><circle cx="358" cy="170" r="19" class="fn sm s1 dash"/><circle cx="358" cy="170" r="7" class="fb"/><circle cx="248" cy="222" r="19" class="fn sm s1 dash"/><circle cx="248" cy="222" r="7" class="fb"/><circle cx="292" cy="222" r="19" class="fn sm s1 dash"/><circle cx="292" cy="222" r="7" class="fb"/>
<text x="292" y="268" class="mid ts fb">ten lonely cases</text>
</g>
<text x="200" y="304" class="mid ts fm" data-l="2" data-fx="up">the majority buys what its peers already use</text>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up" data-d="3">
<rect x="24" y="322" width="352" height="42" rx="12" class="fp"/>
<text x="200" y="349" class="mid ts">10 customers in one field = a reference base</text>
</g>

lines.text: The second reason is even stronger. Buyers do not decide alone. They ask people like themselves.
A dentist asks other dentists. A site manager asks other site managers. A recommendation from a different industry counts for little.
The author Geoffrey Moore described this for technology products. The first buyers love new things. The large majority buys only what its peers already use.
So ten customers in one field are a reference base. Ten customers in ten fields are ten lonely cases.

scenes.title: Start small, then widen
scenes.svg:
<text x="200" y="72" class="mid tx tb" data-l="0" data-fx="pop" data-out="1">Start small</text>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="20" width="352" height="84" rx="14" class="fp"/>
<g transform="translate(34 32)"><circle cx="36" cy="30" r="8" class="fb"/><circle cx="36" cy="30" r="17" class="fn sb s1"/><circle cx="36" cy="30" r="27" class="fn sb s1 dash"/></g>
<text x="122" y="57" class="tm tb">Amazon</text>
<text x="122" y="80" class="ts fm">books only, then everything</text></g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="112" width="352" height="84" rx="14" class="fp"/>
<g transform="translate(34 124)"><circle cx="36" cy="30" r="8" class="fa"/><circle cx="36" cy="30" r="17" class="fn sa s1"/><circle cx="36" cy="30" r="27" class="fn sa s1 dash"/></g>
<text x="122" y="149" class="tm tb">Facebook</text>
<text x="122" y="172" class="ts fm">one university first</text></g>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="204" width="352" height="84" rx="14" class="fp"/>
<g transform="translate(34 216)"><circle cx="36" cy="30" r="8" class="fd"/><circle cx="36" cy="30" r="17" class="fn sd s1"/><circle cx="36" cy="30" r="27" class="fn sd s1 dash"/></g>
<text x="122" y="241" class="tm tb">PayPal</text>
<text x="122" y="264" class="ts fm">a few thousand eBay sellers</text></g>
<text x="356" y="241" class="end ts fd tb" data-l="3" data-fx="up" data-d="3.5">25% in 3 months</text>
<g data-l="4" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="308" width="352" height="42" rx="12" class="fp"/>
<text x="200" y="335" class="mid tm">a large share of a small market</text>
</g>
<text x="200" y="378" class="mid ts fm" data-l="4" data-fx="up" data-d="3">references, pricing power, calm</text>

lines.text: The investor Peter Thiel made a rule out of this: start with a small market that you can dominate.
Amazon started with books only. Not because books were the goal, but because they were easy to list and to ship.
Facebook started with the students of one single university, and won most of them before moving on.
PayPal focused on a few thousand professional sellers on eBay. Within three months, a quarter of them used it.
A large share of a small market beats a tiny share of a huge one. It brings references, pricing power, and the calm to improve the product.

scenes.title: The German version
scenes.svg:
<text x="200" y="38" class="mid tm" data-l="1" data-fx="up">hidden champions</text>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="pop" data-d="0.6"><rect x="30" y="54" width="160" height="34" rx="10" class="fp"/><text x="110" y="76" class="mid ts ">top 3 in the world</text></g><g data-l="1" data-fx="pop" data-d="1.7000000000000002"><rect x="210" y="54" width="160" height="34" rx="10" class="fp"/><text x="290" y="76" class="mid ts ">almost unknown</text></g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">
<text x="107" y="140" class="mid tx tb fa">≈ 3,000</text><text x="107" y="162" class="mid ts fm">worldwide</text>
<text x="293" y="140" class="mid tx tb fb">about half</text><text x="293" y="162" class="mid ts fm">are German</text>
</g>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up">
<rect x="176" y="236" width="48" height="80" rx="8" class="fa"/>
<text x="246" y="298" class="ts fa tb">product: narrow</text>
</g>
<g data-l="4" data-fx="up">
<rect x="40" y="190" width="320" height="40" rx="8" class="fb"/>

</g>

<text x="200" y="365" class="mid ts">narrow in what they do, wide in where they sell</text>
</g>

lines.text: This is not only a story about American start-ups. Germany has its own version.
The economist Hermann Simon calls them hidden champions: firms that are among the top three in the world in their market, and almost unknown to the public.
He counts around three thousand of them worldwide. Roughly half are German.
Their pattern is always the same: a very narrow product focus, combined with selling all over the world.
Narrow in what they do, wide in where they sell. That is how a niche becomes large enough.

scenes.title: The counter-argument
scenes.svg:
<text x="200" y="36" class="mid ts fm" data-l="0" data-fx="up">buying data of many big brands</text>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up">
<text x="40" y="84" class="ts">growth through more buyers</text>
<rect x="40" y="94" width="300" height="18" rx="9" class="fa"/>
<text x="40" y="142" class="ts">growth through more loyalty</text>
<rect x="40" y="152" width="70" height="18" rx="9" class="fm"/>
</g>
<text x="200" y="206" class="mid ts fc tb" data-l="2" data-fx="up">so narrowing cuts off future buyers?</text>
<text x="200" y="236" class="mid ts fm" data-l="3" data-fx="up">measured: established brands, mature markets</text>
<g data-l="4" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="264" width="150" height="56" rx="12" class="fp"/><text x="99" y="290" class="mid ts fb tb">1</text><text x="99" y="308" class="mid ts">win a segment</text>
<g ><line x1="180" y1="292" x2="210" y2="292" class="si"/><polygon points="220,292 210,297.5 210,286.5" class="fi"/></g>
<rect x="226" y="264" width="150" height="56" rx="12" class="fp"/><text x="301" y="290" class="mid ts fa tb">2</text><text x="301" y="308" class="mid ts">widen step by step</text>
<text x="200" y="356" class="mid ts fm">both views fit together as a sequence</text>
</g>

lines.text: Now the other side, and it comes with data. The marketing researcher Byron Sharp studied the buying data of many big brands.
His result: brands grow mainly by winning more buyers, including many who buy only rarely. Not by making a small group more loyal.
Seen this way, narrow targeting is a mistake. You cut yourself off from most of your future buyers.
So who is right? Look at what was measured: established brands in mature markets, with budgets that reach everybody.
A small firm cannot reach everybody. So the two views fit together as a sequence: first win a segment, then widen step by step.

quiz.q: Studies of big brands show: they grow by reaching all buyers, not by narrowing down. A firm with twelve employees reads this. What is the best conclusion?

options.text: The studies cover consumer goods, so they say nothing about small firms
options.why: Too convenient. The core finding, that growth needs new buyers, holds widely. What changes for a small firm is the order of the steps.

options.text: Niche thinking is refuted, so it should address the whole market now
options.why: The finding describes brands that can afford to reach everyone. With twelve people, addressing everyone means reaching almost no one often enough.

options.text: Win a narrow segment first, and widen when broad reach becomes affordable
options.why: The research says where growth comes from in the long run. The reach math says what a small firm can afford today. Together they give an order of steps.

options.text: It should stay in its niche for good, since broad growth needs big budgets
options.why: Half right: broad reach is expensive. But the research also shows where long-term growth comes from. Staying narrow forever puts a ceiling on the firm.

quiz.explain: Two pieces of advice can both be true if they describe different stages. Picture a campfire. To get it burning, you put small, dry twigs close together in one spot. A thick log on its own will not catch. Later, when the fire is strong, you add the big logs, and spreading out is exactly right. Research on big brands describes the big fire: it grows by reaching more and more wood. Advice about niches describes the first minutes: concentrate the little heat you have. The mistake is not choosing one of the two. The mistake is using the rule for the wrong stage.

<circle cx="150" cy="176" r="8" class="fb"/><circle cx="180" cy="176" r="8" class="fb"/><circle cx="210" cy="176" r="8" class="fb"/><circle cx="240" cy="176" r="8" class="fb"/>
<circle cx="60" cy="176" r="8" class="fm"/><circle cx="90" cy="176" r="8" class="fm"/><circle cx="310" cy="176" r="8" class="fm"/><circle cx="340" cy="176" r="8" class="fm"/>
<text x="200" y="216" class="mid ts fb tb">a spotlight: where message and money go</text>
</g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">
<g ><line x1="326" y1="162" x2="275.2" y2="140" class="sa dash"/><polygon points="266,136 277.4,134.9 273,145" class="fa"/></g>
<text x="330" y="118" class="mid ts fa">may still buy</text>
</g>
<text x="200" y="250" class="mid ts fm" data-l="3" data-fx="up">signs of a weak position</text>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="pop" data-d="0.6"><rect x="24" y="266" width="130" height="34" rx="10" class="fp"/><text x="89" y="288" class="mid ts ">“what do you do?”</text></g><g data-l="3" data-fx="pop" data-d="1.7000000000000002"><rect x="162" y="266" width="100" height="34" rx="10" class="fp"/><text x="212" y="288" class="mid ts ">wrong rivals</text></g><g data-l="3" data-fx="pop" data-d="2.8000000000000003"><rect x="270" y="266" width="106" height="34" rx="10" class="fp"/><text x="323" y="288" class="mid ts ">price fights</text></g>
<text x="200" y="352" class="mid ts fm" data-l="0" data-fx="up" data-out="1">“if I focus, I lose the others”</text>

lines.text: This also answers the biggest fear: if I focus, I lose all the other customers.
Positioning is a spotlight, not a fence. It decides where your message and your money go. It does not forbid anyone to buy.
A tool for architects will still be bought by an engineer who finds it. You just did not pay to find him.
The warning signs of a weak position are easy to spot. People ask what exactly you do. They compare you with the wrong rivals. And they argue about the price.

<text x="40" y="78" class="ts">A</text><text x="40" y="108" class="ts">B</text><text x="40" y="138" class="ts">C</text><text x="40" y="168" class="ts">D</text><text x="40" y="198" class="ts">E</text><text x="40" y="228" class="ts">F</text>

<g data-l="1" data-d="4"><rect x="28" y="58" width="344" height="28" rx="8" class="fn sb"/><rect x="28" y="148" width="344" height="28" rx="8" class="fn sb"/><rect x="28" y="208" width="344" height="28" rx="8" class="fn sb"/></g>
<text x="200" y="266" class="mid ts fb tb" data-l="2" data-fx="up">what do A, D and F share? A situation</text>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="pop" data-d="0.6"><rect x="24" y="290" width="104" height="34" rx="10" class="fp"/><text x="76" y="312" class="mid ts ">list by name?</text></g><g data-l="3" data-fx="pop" data-d="1.7000000000000002"><rect x="136" y="290" width="134" height="34" rx="10" class="fp"/><text x="203" y="312" class="mid ts ">talk to each other?</text></g><g data-l="3" data-fx="pop" data-d="2.8000000000000003"><rect x="278" y="290" width="98" height="34" rx="10" class="fp"/><text x="327" y="312" class="mid ts ">urgent?</text></g>
<text x="200" y="356" class="mid ts fm" data-l="3" data-fx="up" data-d="4">three tests for a segment</text>

lines.text: How do you find your segment? Not by brainstorming. Look at the customers you already have.
Who bought quickly, paid without haggling, stayed, and recommended you? Put those names on one list.
Then ask what they share. Usually it is not age or company size. It is a situation: a certain problem at a certain moment.
Then test the group with three questions. Can you list its members by name? Do they talk to each other? And is the problem urgent enough to have a budget?

scenes.svg:
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up">

<text x="34" y="78" class="ts">our product is a <tspan class="fb tb">[category]</tspan></text>
<text x="34" y="104" class="ts">that delivers <tspan class="fd tb">[benefit]</tspan>.</text>
<text x="34" y="130" class="ts">Unlike <tspan class="fc tb">[alternative]</tspan>, it <tspan class="fe tb">[difference]</tspan>.</text>
</g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="158" width="352" height="138" rx="14" class="fp"/>
<text x="40" y="186" class="ts">For <tspan class="fa">small architecture offices</tspan></text>
<text x="40" y="210" class="ts">that <tspan class="fa">lose hours on site reports</tspan>:</text>
<text x="40" y="234" class="ts">a <tspan class="fb">reporting app</tspan>, <tspan class="fd">photos become reports</tspan>.</text>
<text x="40" y="258" class="ts">Unlike <tspan class="fc">Word and Excel</tspan>,</text>
<text x="40" y="282" class="ts"><tspan class="fe">it works on the building site</tspan>.</text>
</g>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="318" width="352" height="42" rx="12" class="fp"/>
<text x="200" y="345" class="mid ts">every blank you cannot fill is a gap</text>
</g>
<text x="200" y="26" class="mid ts fm" data-l="0" data-fx="up">Geoffrey Moore’s template</text>

lines.text: Finally, write it down in one sentence. Geoffrey Moore’s template still works.
For a certain customer with a certain problem, our product is a certain category that delivers a certain benefit. Unlike the main alternative, it does one thing differently.
An example. For small architecture offices that lose hours on site reports: a reporting app that turns photos into finished reports. Unlike Word and Excel, it works on the building site.
If you cannot fill in every blank, the gap shows you exactly where your positioning is still open.

scenes.title: When to widen
scenes.svg:
<g data-l="0" data-fx="up"><circle cx="200" cy="250" r="20" class="fk sa"/><text x="200" y="255" class="mid ts fa tb">1</text><text x="200" y="298" class="mid ts fa">your niche, won</text></g>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up">
<circle cx="152" cy="180" r="20" class="fk sm"/><text x="152" y="185" class="mid ts fm tb"></text><circle cx="248" cy="180" r="20" class="fk sm"/><text x="248" y="185" class="mid ts fm tb"></text><circle cx="104" cy="110" r="20" class="fk sm"/><text x="104" y="115" class="mid ts fm tb"></text><circle cx="200" cy="110" r="20" class="fk sm"/><text x="200" y="115" class="mid ts fm tb"></text><circle cx="296" cy="110" r="20" class="fk sm"/><text x="296" y="115" class="mid ts fm tb"></text>
</g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">
<circle cx="152" cy="180" r="20" class="fk sb"/><text x="152" y="185" class="mid ts fb tb">2</text><circle cx="248" cy="180" r="20" class="fk sb"/><text x="248" y="185" class="mid ts fb tb">2</text>
<g ><line x1="188" y1="232" x2="170.5" y2="206.6" class="sb"/><polygon points="166,200 174.2,204.1 166.9,209.1" class="fb"/></g><g ><line x1="212" y1="232" x2="229.5" y2="206.6" class="sb"/><polygon points="234,200 233.1,209.1 225.8,204.1" class="fb"/></g>
<text x="200" y="54" class="mid ts fb tb">next: the neighbours</text>
<text x="200" y="74" class="mid ts fm">they know your customers, similar problem</text>
</g>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up">
<circle cx="356" cy="250" r="18" class="fn sc dash"/>
<text x="330" y="298" class="mid ts fc">distant market:</text><text x="330" y="316" class="mid ts fc">start from zero</text>
</g>
<g data-l="3" data-fx="up" data-d="3">
<rect x="24" y="338" width="352" height="42" rx="12" class="fp"/>
<text x="200" y="365" class="mid ts">references and product must still count</text>
</g>

lines.text: And when do you leave the niche? When you lead it, and growth there slows down.
Moore compares it to bowling. The first pin, when it falls, knocks over the ones standing next to it.
So the next segment should stand next to the first one: people who know your current customers, and who have a similar problem.
That way, your references and your product still count. A jump into a distant market means starting from zero again.

quiz.q: A firm leads its niche: software for small architecture offices. Growth there slows down. Which next step fits the bowling-pin logic best?

options.text: All small service firms, to use the strong brand in a much larger market
options.why: The brand is strong among architects only. In the broad market nobody has heard of it, and its references mean little there.

options.text: Hospitals, because they have the largest budgets for software
options.why: The budget is attractive, but nothing carries over: not the references, not the product, not the contacts. That is a restart, not a next pin.

options.text: Small engineering offices that work with these architects on the same projects
options.why: They know the current customers, so the references count. And their problem is similar, so the product still fits. That is the pin next door.

options.text: The same offices, with a second product for an unrelated problem
options.why: The customers stay, which is worth a lot. But an unrelated product has to be built and proven from zero. Only one of the two assets carries over.

quiz.explain: Think of a climber on a wall. A safe move keeps three points on the rock and moves only one hand or one foot. A firm that leaves its niche has two holds: customers who trust it, and a product that works. A move to a neighbouring group keeps both: the new customers have heard of you from the old ones, and the product needs only small changes. A new product for old customers lets go of one hold. A distant market with a big budget lets go of both at once. The question to ask about every next step is: what do I get to keep?

scenes.title: The short version
scenes.svg:
<g data-l="0" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="20" width="352" height="84" rx="14" class="fp"/>
<g transform="translate(34 32)"><rect x="10" y="8" width="52" height="44" rx="6" class="fn sa"/><circle cx="36" cy="30" r="8" class="fa"/></g>

<text x="122" y="80" class="ts fm">for whom, instead of what, why better</text></g>
<g data-l="1" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="112" width="352" height="84" rx="14" class="fp"/>
<g transform="translate(34 124)"><circle cx="36" cy="30" r="22" class="fn sb"/><circle cx="36" cy="30" r="8" class="fb"/></g>
<text x="122" y="149" class="tm tb">Small enough to be known</text>
<text x="122" y="172" class="ts fm">start from the real alternative</text></g>
<g data-l="2" data-fx="up">
<rect x="24" y="204" width="352" height="84" rx="14" class="fp"/>
<g transform="translate(34 216)"><circle cx="22" cy="38" r="12" class="fn sd"/><circle cx="50" cy="22" r="12" class="fn sd dash"/></g>
<text x="122" y="241" class="tm tb">Win it, then the neighbour</text>
<text x="122" y="264" class="ts fm">references carry you over</text></g>
<text x="200" y="330" class="mid tl tb fb" data-l="2" data-fx="up" data-d="3">“for everyone” comes last</text>

lines.text: The short version. Positioning is the frame: for whom, instead of what, and why better.
Start with the real alternative, not with yourself. Choose a segment small enough that you can become known in it.
Win it, collect references, then move to the neighbour. “For everyone” comes last, not first.

takeaways: Positioning is not a slogan. It is the frame around a product: for whom, instead of what, and why better.
People always compare. If you do not choose the comparison, your customers choose one, and usually an unfavourable one.
Start with the real alternative (often Excel or doing nothing), then your difference, its benefit, the group that cares most, and the category.
A small market multiplies limited effort: you reach each customer several times, and customers in one field recommend you to each other.
Research on big brands shows that long-term growth needs many new buyers. For a small firm this means a sequence: win a segment first, then widen.
Widen to the neighbouring segment, where your references and your product still count.
sources: April Dunford: Obviously Awesome (2019), the five components of positioning
Geoffrey Moore: Crossing the Chasm (1991), reference customers, the positioning template and the bowling-pin strategy
Peter Thiel: Zero to One (2014), start small and monopolize; the Amazon, Facebook and PayPal examples
